title: Design a Distributed Cache
summary: A cache that is itself a distributed system — sharding, invalidation propagation, and the hot-key problem at cluster scale.

slides.markdown:
Build the shared cache tier itself — the thing other topics in this group casually put "a cache" in front of. At cluster scale, a cache stops being one fast box and becomes its own distributed system: sharded across nodes, with invalidation that has to propagate correctly and a hot-key problem that can exceed any single node's capacity.

This is Memcached-Cluster or Redis-Cluster territory: the algorithm (LRU, TTL) is the easy part; the distributed-systems shape around it is the interview.

**Functional:** `get`/`set`/`delete` keys, with a configurable eviction policy and per-key TTLs, serving many independent services as a shared tier.

**Non-functional:** a target hit ratio (often 90%+ for the workload to matter), a staleness tolerance (how out-of-date is an acceptable cached value), and predictable low latency even as the cluster grows.

The staleness tolerance is worth stating explicitly up front — it directly decides how aggressive invalidation needs to be later in the design.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: working-set size vs node memory
slides.markdown:
If the hot working set is 500GB and each cache node has 64GB of usable memory, you need at least 8 shards just to hold the data, before adding any headroom for uneven distribution or growth — a common rule of thumb is to size for 60-70% target memory utilization per node, pushing the real number closer to 12-14 shards.

This number should come from the actual working set (what's *repeatedly* accessed), not total data volume — a cache sized for total data volume is usually wildly over-provisioned, since most systems have a small hot subset.

`get(key)`, `set(key, value, ttl?)`, `delete(key)` — plus a versioned-invalidation variant, `set(key, value, version)`, so a stale write racing a newer one can be detected and dropped rather than silently overwriting a fresher value.

Keeping the surface Memcached-simple (rather than adding transactions or complex queries) is deliberate: a shared cache tier used by many unrelated services needs to stay predictable and fast, not become a second database.

slides.sectionTitle: Sharding keys across cache nodes with consistent hashing
slides.markdown:
Exactly like the key-value store topic, keys are distributed across nodes using consistent hashing with virtual nodes, so adding or removing a cache node only reassigns a bounded slice of the keyspace.

The stakes are different here, though: a key-value store's ring reassignment is a durability question (data must be re-replicated); a cache's reassignment is a performance question (reassigned keys are simply cold on their new node) — losing a cache entry is an inconvenience, not data loss, since the source of truth lives elsewhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: client routing to the right shard via a hash ring
slides.markdown:
![Client-side routing library hashing a key and going directly to the owning shard on the ring](assets/cache-client-side-routing.svg)

Most distributed caches route on the **client side**: the calling application links a small library that knows the ring topology and computes which shard owns a key locally, sending the request directly there.

This avoids adding a central proxy/router as a bottleneck and single point of failure on every single cache operation — at the cost of every client needing to stay aware of ring topology changes.

assets.alt: Client-side routing library hashing a key and going directly to the owning shard on the ring

slides.sectionTitle: Cache invalidation across nodes: TTL vs explicit broadcast
slides.markdown:
| | TTL expiry | Explicit invalidation broadcast |
|---|---|---|
| Staleness window | Bounded by TTL — can serve stale data until it expires | Near-immediate once the broadcast lands |
| Complexity | Trivial — just set an expiry | Needs a pub/sub or messaging layer to reach every node holding the key |
| Failure mode | Fails safe — worst case is serving slightly stale data | A missed broadcast leaves a node stale indefinitely, with no self-correction |

**How to decide:** use TTL as the baseline always, since it fails safe. Layer explicit invalidation on top only for data where staleness has a real cost (e.g. a price change) — and even then, keep a TTL as a backstop in case a broadcast is missed.

slides.sectionTitle: The hot-key problem: one key exceeding a single node's capacity
slides.markdown:
Consistent hashing balances keys evenly across nodes, but a single extremely popular key (a viral post's metadata, a flash-sale product) can still generate more read traffic than one node can serve — no amount of rebalancing helps, because the key can only live on one shard's worth of nodes at a time.

This is the cache-specific version of the hot-partition problem seen in the key-value store topic, but sharper here: since the cache's whole job is absorbing read load, a hot key defeats that purpose exactly where it matters most.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: hot-key mitigation with local caching and key-splitting
slides.markdown:
![Hot key split into suffixed keys across nodes, plus a local in-process cache in front](assets/cache-hot-key-splitting.svg)

Two complementary fixes: **key-splitting** stores the same value under several suffixed keys (`key#0`..`key#N`) spread across different nodes, and clients pick a suffix at random, spreading one hot key's load across N nodes instead of one. **Local (in-process) caching** on each app server holds the very hottest keys directly in application memory, skipping the network hop to the distributed cache entirely for the most extreme cases.

Both trade a little staleness or memory duplication for taking pressure off the single node that would otherwise own the hot key.

assets.alt: Hot key split into suffixed keys across nodes, plus a local in-process cache in front

slides.sectionTitle: Node failure and rebalancing without a stampede on the database
slides.markdown:
When a cache node fails, the keys it owned become cache misses on their new owner (per the ring) — if that's a large fraction of the keyspace, the backing database can suddenly see a spike of requests it hasn't seen in a while, since those keys were previously served entirely from cache.

Mitigation: stagger cache warmup for a newly-added or recovered node (pre-populate from the database gradually rather than serving cold and forcing every request through), and keep per-node request-rate limiting to the database so one node's cold cache can't unbound the load it forwards downstream.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a full cache-cluster restart causing a thundering herd
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We can safely restart the whole cache cluster during a maintenance window — it's just a cache, the database still has the real data."

**Why it's wrong:** restarting every node at once means every key in the cluster is a miss simultaneously — the backing database, which had been shielded from nearly all read traffic, suddenly receives the *entire* read load at once, often enough to overload or crash it, which is a much worse outage than the cache restart itself.

**Correct model:** restart cache nodes in a staggered rolling fashion, never all at once, and consider pre-warming a replacement cluster from the database before cutting traffic over, so the database never sees a full-traffic spike.
